english_translation: In our home region there are tall mountains that are wonderful to see.

dialogue.shona: Kwedu kune makomo marefu anonakidza kuona.
dialogue.english: In our home region there are tall mountains that are wonderful to see.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Kwedu [kwedu] • kune [to / at ne] • makomo [mountains] • marefu [plural refu] • anonakidza [he/she nakidza] • kuona [to / at ona]

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anonakidza')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anonakidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('Kwedu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'Kwedu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

grammar_notes.title: Expressing 'Has/Have' and 'There Is/Are' ('-ne' & 'pane / kune')
grammar_notes.content: Shona does not use a separate verb like 'have'; instead, it combines a subject prefix with '-ne' ('with'). For people: 'ndine' (I have), 'une' (you have), 'ane' (he/she has), 'tine' (we have), 'vane' (they have). For things, the prefix matches the object: 'imba ine...' ('the house has...'), 'rori rine...' ('the truck has...'). When combined with the location prefixes 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-', it means 'there is / there are': 'pane' ('there is right here'), 'kune' ('there is in that area'), and 'mune' ('there is inside').
grammar_notes.rule: Person/Thing + -ne = has/have (tine = we have, ine = it has) | pane / kune / mune = there is / there are

cultural_notes.title: Zimbabwe's Natural Landscape & Wildlife
cultural_notes.content: Zimbabwe is renowned for its dramatic landscapes—from the eastern highlands and balancing granite hills ('makomo') to great rivers ('rwizi') like the Zambezi and rich wildlife parks home to rhinoceroses ('zvipembere'), elephants ('nzou'), and diverse birdlife ('shiri'). In both rural and suburban homes, dogs ('imbwa') are kept as loyal watchdogs that alert the household at night.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this future weather forecast: 'Mangwana zuva ______ zvakanaka.' (Tomorrow the sun will shine brightly.)
active_exercises.explanation: 'Zuva' (sun) takes the prefix 'ri-' + future marker '-cha-' + '-buda' (come out/shine) -> 'richabuda'.

active_exercises.prompt: If a farmer says 'Gore rino takawana goho guru pamunda pedu', what happened?
options: They are waiting for the rain to start next month
They obtained a big harvest from their field this year
The river flooded and washed away the bridge
A strong wind blew from the east all afternoon
active_exercises.correct_answer: They obtained a big harvest from their field this year
active_exercises.explanation: 'Takawana' = 'we obtained/got', 'goho guru' = 'a big harvest', 'pamunda pedu' = 'from our field'.

active_exercises.prompt: Which phrase correctly translates 'three books' in Shona? (Hint: 'mabhuku' is a 'ma-' plural noun.)
active_exercises.explanation: The number stem '-tatu' (three) takes the 'ma-' prefix to match 'mabhuku' -> 'mabhuku matatu'.
